stem: What are mutually exclusive projects?

options.content: Projects of which only one can be chosen
options.rationale: Correct: choosing one rules out the other.

options.content: Projects that must all be undertaken together
options.rationale: That describes linked projects.

options.content: Projects that have no cost
options.rationale: Mutually exclusive projects can have any cost.

options.content: Projects with identical cash flows
options.rationale: They may differ in cash flows; exclusivity is about the choice.

explanation: Mutually exclusive projects are alternatives: the business can undertake only one.

stem: Which investment appraisal technique uses accounting profit rather than cash flows?

options.content: Accounting rate of return
options.rationale: Correct: ARR is based on average profit.

options.content: Payback period
options.rationale: Payback uses cash flows.

options.content: Net present value
options.rationale: NPV discounts cash flows.

options.content: Internal rate of return on capital
options.rationale: IRR is also based on cash flows.

explanation: ARR uses profits after depreciation; the other three use cash flows.

stem: Which is a non-financial factor that might influence an investment decision?

options.content: The net present value of the project at its cost of capital
options.rationale: NPV is a financial measure.

options.content: The number of jobs created in the community
options.rationale: Correct: employment is a non-financial factor.

options.content: The payback period in years
options.rationale: Payback is a financial measure.

options.content: The accounting rate of return
options.rationale: ARR is a financial measure.

explanation: Employment, environment, reputation and strategy are examples of non-financial factors.

stem: Two mutually exclusive projects have different sizes. Project P has the higher IRR but a lower NPV than Project Q. Which is generally preferred on financial grounds?

options.content: Project P, because a higher percentage is always better
options.rationale: A high percentage on a small project may add less value.

options.content: Project Q, because it adds the greater value in dollars
options.rationale: Correct: NPV measures the value added.

options.content: Neither, because the methods disagree
options.rationale: A choice can be made by ranking on NPV.

options.content: Project P, because it must be cheaper
options.rationale: Cost is not the issue; value added is.

explanation: For mutually exclusive projects the NPV shows the extra wealth created, so the higher NPV is normally chosen.

stem: What does sensitivity analysis show?

options.content: The exact future cash flows of a project over its whole life
options.rationale: The future is not known exactly.

options.content: The cost of capital of the business
options.rationale: The cost of capital is determined separately.

options.content: How much the result changes if a forecast changes
options.rationale: Correct: it tests the effect of an assumption.

options.content: The tax payable on the project
options.rationale: Tax is not what the analysis shows.

explanation: Sensitivity analysis changes one variable and recalculates the NPV to show how robust the decision is.

stem: Why are projects with longer lives generally considered more risky?

options.content: Longer projects always cost more to start
options.rationale: Cost at the start does not depend on life.

options.content: Discount factors are larger for later years than for earlier ones
options.rationale: Discount factors are smaller for later years.

options.content: Depreciation is higher for longer projects
options.rationale: Depreciation per year is usually lower for longer lives.

options.content: Forecasts of distant cash flows are less reliable
options.rationale: Correct: uncertainty increases with time.

explanation: It is harder to forecast inflows many years ahead, so the risk is greater.

stem: A business must choose between a project with a positive NPV that harms a local river and one with a smaller NPV that does not. Which is the BEST approach?

options.content: Always choose the higher NPV, because only money matters
options.rationale: Non-financial factors may change the decision.

options.content: Always choose the project with the lower NPV, because it is much safer
options.rationale: Safety is not guaranteed by a lower NPV.

options.content: Reject both without looking at the figures
options.rationale: The figures are needed for the decision.

options.content: Weigh the extra NPV against the environmental and reputation costs
options.rationale: Correct: financial and non-financial factors should both be considered.

explanation: Good decisions balance the financial result with environmental, social and strategic effects.
hints: Both financial and non-financial factors matter.

stem: Depreciation is deducted from cash flows when calculating the NPV of a project.
explanation: False. Depreciation is not a cash flow, so it is not deducted in NPV, payback or IRR.

stem: A project can have a positive NPV and a long payback period at the same time.
explanation: True. NPV considers the whole life of the project while payback only looks at the recovery time.

stem: Match each factor to the investment appraisal point it illustrates.

left.content: The inflows may fall short of the forecast
Only one of two machines can be bought
The project creates jobs in the community
Depreciation reduces profit but not cash

right.content: Difference between profit and cash flow

explanation: Each statement illustrates a different aspect of project evaluation.

stem: Complete the sentence.

payload.template: When payback and NPV give different rankings, the business should usually prefer the project with the higher {{blank:a}} because it measures the {{blank:b}} added.

explanation: NPV measures the value added in dollars.

stem: Name the technique that recalculates the NPV after changing a forecast to see how much the decision depends on it.
explanation: It is sensitivity analysis.

stem: A project has a net present value of US\$9,600. The total present value of its inflows is US\$64,000. By what percentage could all the inflows fall before the NPV reaches zero? Give your answer to one decimal place.
explanation: 9,600 ÷ 64,000 × 100 = 15.0%. Dividing by the outlay (54,400) would give 17.6%, which is the wrong base.
workedSolution: 1. 9,600 ÷ 64,000 × 100 = 15.0%. Dividing by the outlay (54,400) would give 17.6%, which is the wrong base.
hints: NPV ÷ total present value of inflows.

stem: A project costs US\$90,000, brings net cash inflows of US\$24,000 a year for 5 years and has no residual value. Depreciation is straight line. Calculate the annual accounting profit.
explanation: Depreciation = 90,000 ÷ 5 = 18,000 a year. Profit = 24,000 - 18,000 = US\$6,000. The cash inflow (US\$24,000) is not the profit.
workedSolution: 1. Depreciation = 90,000 ÷ 5 = 18,000 a year. Profit = 24,000 - 18,000 = US\$6,000. The cash inflow (US\$24,000) is not the profit.
hints: Depreciation is not a cash flow, but it is a deduction from profit.

stem: A project costing US\$100,000 has inflows with a total present value of US\$120,000. Calculate the net present value if every inflow turns out to be 15% lower than forecast.
hints: Reduce the present value of the inflows by 15% first.

stem: Explain why a project's accounting profit differs from its net cash flow.

points.description: Accounting profit is after depreciation, which is not a cash flow
Timing differences: sales and costs may not be paid or received in the same year
Capital spending is not an expense in profit but is a cash outflow when paid

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Profit is after deducting depreciation, which is not a cash flow. Timing of receipts and payments also differs, and capital spending is a cash outflow but not an expense in the period.

explanation: One mark for each reason.

stem: Explain two ways in which a business can allow for risk in its investment appraisal.

points.description: Use sensitivity analysis to see how far the inflows can fall before the NPV is zero
Developed: a project that is very sensitive to small falls is risky
Use a higher discount rate or a shorter payback requirement for risky projects
Developed: a higher rate reduces the present value of distant, uncertain flows

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The business can test the NPV with lower inflows to see how sensitive the result is. It can also use a higher discount rate or a shorter payback target for risky projects, which reduces the value placed on distant, uncertain flows.

explanation: One mark for each method and one for developing each.
hints: One method about testing, one about adjusting the criteria.

stem: A manager says 'We should choose the project with the shortest payback period.' Evaluate this advice.

points.description: A short payback returns cash quickly and reduces risk
It is useful when the business is short of cash
But payback ignores cash flows after the payback point and the time value of money, so a better project may be rejected
Judgement: use payback as a screening or liquidity test, but base the choice on NPV with risk and non-financial factors

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Shorter payback means quicker recovery of cash and lower risk, which matters when cash is short. However, it ignores later cash flows and the time value of money, so the choice should be based on NPV, using payback only as a liquidity test.

explanation: One mark for each point.

stem:
Sipho Transport in Bulawayo is choosing between Truck X and Truck Y. Each costs US\$70,000 and has no residual value. The net cash inflows are: Truck X US\$38,000, US\$34,000, US\$22,000 in years 1 to 3; Truck Y US\$18,000, US\$26,000, US\$34,000, US\$40,000 in years 1 to 4. Inflows arise evenly during each year. The cost of capital is 16%.

| Year | Discount factor at 16% |
| --- | ---: |
| 1 | 0.862 |
| 2 | 0.743 |
| 3 | 0.641 |
| 4 | 0.552 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the payback period of Truck X, in years to two decimal places.
parts.explanation: After 1 year 38,000 is recovered; 32,000 remains. 32,000 ÷ 34,000 = 0.94. Payback = 1.94 years.
parts.workedSolution: 1. After 1 year 38,000 is recovered; 32,000 remains. 32,000 ÷ 34,000 = 0.94. Payback = 1.94 years.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the ARR of Truck Y, to one decimal place.
parts.explanation: Total profit = 118,000 - 70,000 = 48,000; average = 12,000; average investment = 35,000. ARR = 34.3%.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Total profit = 118,000 - 70,000 = 48,000; average = 12,000; average investment = 35,000. ARR = 34.3%.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the NPV of Truck X.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the NPV of Truck Y.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Which measure shows the value added by each truck in dollars?

options.content: Payback period
options.rationale: Payback measures time.

options.content: Accounting rate of return
options.rationale: ARR is a percentage of profits.

options.content: Net present value
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Depreciation
options.rationale: Depreciation is a cost allocation.

parts.explanation: NPV is the value added in today's dollars.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Evaluate the two trucks and recommend which to buy.

points.description: Truck X pays back faster (1.94 years against 2.76 years), which reduces risk and helps liquidity
Truck Y has the higher ARR (34.3% against 22.9%) and the higher NPV (US\$8,708 against US\$2,120)
Truck X's NPV is small, so a small fall in its inflows would make the NPV negative; Truck Y has more margin for error
Y relies on year 4 inflows, which are less certain than earlier ones
Recommend Truck Y, on the higher NPV, unless cash is very short or the year 4 forecasts are doubtful; mention a non-financial factor such as reliability or maintenance

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Truck X pays back faster, but Truck Y has the higher ARR and a much higher NPV (US\$8,708 against US\$2,120), and its NPV can better withstand falls in inflows. Y's year 4 flows are less certain, so reliability and maintenance should be checked, but Truck Y should be bought.

hints: Compare each technique, then give a decision.

explanation: This item compares two projects with several techniques and asks for a recommendation.
hints: Use the factors supplied for NPV.

stem: Rudo Dairy in Masvingo is considering a cooling plant costing US\$45,000. At the cost of capital of 20% the present value of the inflows is US\$51,300. The owner is worried that the milk price may fall.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage fall in all inflows that would make the NPV zero, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: If every inflow is 15% lower than forecast, by how much is the NPV below zero? (Amount only.)

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Advise the owner whether to go ahead, referring to the sensitivity results and one non-financial factor.

points.description: The NPV is positive, so the plant is expected to earn more than 20%
But the NPV becomes negative if inflows fall by more than 12.3%, so the margin for error is small
A fall of 15% would give a negative NPV of US\$1,395
Non-financial factor (reduced spoilage and better milk quality, or dependence on electricity supply) and a clear decision

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The NPV of US\$6,300 suggests acceptance, but inflows need fall by only 12.3% to remove it, and a 15% fall gives a negative NPV. The owner should go ahead only if the milk price is reasonably secure, and should consider the benefit of less spoilage and the risk of power cuts.

explanation: This item tests sensitivity analysis and a reasoned recommendation.
hints: NPV = present value of inflows - outlay.
Fall that removes the NPV = NPV ÷ present value of inflows.
